title: Stockton, 1912
hook: Sikh farmworkers open the first gurdwara in the United States in California
carry: a door in a new land

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirat: gurdwaras built from mill lumber, and your line, honest work, far away. Today we go south, down the coast, to the farms of California. Day three hundred fifteen.

California's Central Valley, about 1910. Flat fields to the horizon, heat shimmering off the dirt. Men from Punjab, many of them Sikh, have come down from Canada and across from Asia to work the farms: picking fruit, clearing land, laying irrigation ditches. It's familiar work. Punjab means five rivers, and these are farmers who know water and soil. But on a Sunday, there's nowhere to go. The nearest gurdwara is far up the coast in Vancouver, days away by train. So a few of them decide to make one. Today: Stockton.
screen: `THE CENTRAL VALLEY, ABOUT 1910.` → `FARMERS WHO KNOW WATER AND SOIL.` → `NOWHERE TO GO ON SUNDAY.`

segments.voice: In 1912, Sikh farmworkers formed the Pacific Coast Khalsa Diwan Society and opened a gurdwara in Stockton, a farm town in the Central Valley. It was the first gurdwara in the United States. It began modestly, and years later a new building went up beside the first. For decades it was the only one in the country, the place Sikhs traveled to from all over the West for gurpurabs, weddings and news from home. Think about the word gurdwara. Gur, the Guru. Dwara, a door. The Guru's door. And that's exactly what Stockton was: a door in a new land. Through it, lonely men found a sangat, a hot meal at langar, a bed for the night. Through it, too, came politics. Some Sikhs and other Indians in California were campaigning for India's freedom from British rule, and Stockton's gurdwara became a meeting place for them. Life outside the door was hard. Laws kept most Indian women from coming, and restricted who the men could marry and whether they could own land. In southern California, many Punjabi men married Mexican women, and their children grew up in families that mixed Punjabi and Spanish, gurdwara and church. Their children were sometimes called Mexican-Hindus, and some of them came to Stockton for the big gatherings. Looking back at this week: the library that was lost, November 1984, the long wait, how the panth remembers, leaving Punjab, the sawmills, and now Stockton. From loss, to a door opened in a new land.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find a gurdwara near you. If you have your phone, look up the nearest gurdwara to where you are right now. Just find it on a map. Notice how far it is, and what street it's on. You don't have to go. Then put the phone down, settle, and breathe. Picture its door, open, with shoes lined up outside and someone serving tea inside. Think of the farmworkers in Stockton who made the first one. The bell holds the time.
Stockton. The California farm town where Sikh farmworkers opened the first gurdwara in the United States, in 1912.

Your line: a door in a new land. Today, when you walk through a door you take for granted, at home, at work or at a place you love, think of who first built it, and who it lets in. Day three hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Gurdwaras across the United States welcome visitors to kirtan and langar; the Stockton gurdwara, the oldest in the country, still serves a sangat today.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gurdwara is a Sikh church.
what it means: the Guru's door: a place of the Guru, a sangat, a kitchen and a bed, a door in a new land.
what a scholar hears: Stockton's gurdwara (1912) was linked with the Ghadar movement; Punjabi-Mexican families formed under immigration and marriage laws of the time.

Audit (10% sample): 'no gurdwara for a thousand miles' was loose (Vancouver's 1908 gurdwara was roughly that far by rail); now 'the nearest gurdwara is far up the coast in Vancouver'. Replaced the filler 'every one of those families found some way through' with a concrete line; the 'Mexican-Hindu' label and the families attending Stockton gatherings follow Karen Leonard's work, confirm. The carry's 'be a door for someone new' repeated day 316's welcome-a-newcomer practice; it now asks the listener to notice who built a familiar door and who it lets in.
